Elm Quay Housing's maintenance team spent eight weeks testing a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two buildings. Its supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week of preparation. This case shows what the preparation took, what the trial figures show and what they leave open.

By Thomas Barregren

In September 2025, the maintenance team at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats, decided to test a shared repair log in two of its buildings. The trial that followed lasted eight weeks. It left the team with a first set of figures, advice about preparation and a question to settle before it goes further.

## Elm Quay wanted its shifts to share one picture

Before the trial, telephone reports and emails were stored separately. “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done,” maintenance supervisor Maya Lind wrote in an email interview.

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether its log could show the status of each repair.

## The maintenance team designed its own categories

The team kept telephone reporting open for residents. “The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log,” Lind wrote. Svale also configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions.

Lind also offered advice about that work. “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## The trial note does not credit software for quicker assignment

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says 31 repair reports were entered. The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

The median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. There are no measurements of cost, resident satisfaction or completion time.

## Lind would repeat the trial, with an extra week to prepare

Lind's assessment does not rest on the figures. “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

She did not recommend Svale to every housing company.

## Elm Quay will check larger repairs before deciding

The trial has not yet been expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs. Operations managers considering a shared repair log of their own can read the [implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).
EOF

# Elm Quay's trial puts repair reports in one view

Elm Quay Housing's maintenance team spent eight weeks testing a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two buildings. Its supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week of preparation. This case shows what the preparation took, what the trial figures show and what they leave open.

By Thomas Barregren

In September 2025, the maintenance team at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats, decided to test a shared repair log in two of its buildings. The trial that followed lasted eight weeks. It left the team with a first set of figures, advice about preparation and a question to settle before it goes further.

## Elm Quay wanted its shifts to share one picture

Before the trial, telephone reports and emails were stored separately. “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done,” maintenance supervisor Maya Lind wrote in an email interview.

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether its log could show the status of each repair.

## The maintenance team designed its own categories

The team kept telephone reporting open for residents. “The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log,” Lind wrote. Svale also configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions.

Lind also offered advice about that work. “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## The trial note does not credit software for quicker assignment

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says 31 repair reports were entered. The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

The median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. There are no measurements of cost, resident satisfaction or completion time.

## Lind would repeat the trial, with an extra week to prepare

Lind's assessment does not rest on the figures. “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

She did not recommend Svale to every housing company.

## Elm Quay will check larger repairs before deciding

The trial has not yet been expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs. Operations managers considering a shared repair log of their own can read the [implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).

# Source comparison report 2: Elm Quay draft

Draft: scratch/write-run.9ylQ/draft.md
Material: work/source.md (Brief, Material, Forbidden inferences / judging)
Draft language: en_US. Source language: English. No quotation is translated, so there are no translation findings. The byline is out of scope, as instructed.

## A. Claim accounting

Each row pairs a draft passage (D) with the source passage (S) it rests on, then gives the difference and the verdict.

### Title

1. D: "Elm Quay's trial puts repairs in one view"
   S: "Having one view of the reports helps us" (Lind); "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."; "testing whether the log could show the status of each repair"; "It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
   Difference: The thing named and the speaker both change. The source's "one view" is Lind's, and it covers "the reports". The title states it in the narrator's voice and applies it to "repairs" with no scope limit. Present-tense "puts" is ordinary headline tense, and Lind's present "helps us" covers it. **Finding 1.**

### Standfirst

2. D: "Elm Quay Housing's maintenance team spent eight weeks testing a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two buildings."
   S: "its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings"; "It chose Svale Systems"; "The trial lasted eight weeks."
   Difference: none material. Supported.

3. D: "Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind would run the trial again, with an extra week of preparation."
   S: "I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation." Also "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment."
   Difference: "run" stands for "choose to do". The conditional "would" and the reservation (the extra week) are both kept. The draft reports this as her stance, not as a fact about the trial. Supported.

4. D: "This case shows what the preparation took, what the trial figures show and what they leave open."
   S: No direct source. This is the author's framing of the article's contents. The article does report the preparation elements (categories, configuration, training of six staff, Lind's remark on time spent), the figures and the gaps ("There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements."). "they" is third-person plural and refers to the figures, with no gender. It is not an independent factual claim. Not a finding.

### Opening paragraph

5. D: "In September 2025, the maintenance team at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats, decided to test a shared repair log in two of its buildings."
   S: "Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings."
   Difference: "two of its buildings" adds the possessive and implies Elm Quay has more than two buildings. Lind's "before the next building starts" and the managed stock of 640 flats cover this. "its" is neuter singular and refers to the company. Supported.

6. D: "The trial that followed lasted eight weeks."
   S: "The trial lasted eight weeks."
   Difference: "that followed" only orders the decision before the trial. Supported.

7. D: "It left the team with a first set of figures, advice about preparation and a question to settle before it goes further."
   S: The trial note figures; Lind: "I would set that time aside before the next building starts." and "I would leave an extra week for preparation."; "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
   Difference:
   - "first set of figures" reads as the initial figures. It does not assert that more will follow, and it is not a finding.
   - "a question to settle before it goes further" matches the source: the decision comes after the check.
   - "advice about preparation" gives Lind's first-person conditional statements the speech act of advice. **Finding 2.**

### "Elm Quay wanted its shifts to share one picture"

8. D (heading): "Elm Quay wanted its shifts to share one picture"
   S: "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."
   Difference: The subject is "Elm Quay" where the source says "The team". The source calls the team "its own maintenance team", and the brief says "The customer, Elm Quay Housing, should remain the acting party." The metonymy is supported. "share one picture" is a figurative rendering of "see the same information". Supported.

9. D: "Before the trial, telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
   S: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
   Supported.

10. D: "“We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done,” maintenance supervisor Maya Lind wrote in an email interview."
    S: "“We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. …”"; "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind"; "All interviews occurred by email".
    Difference: The quotation is exact. It is the first sentence of the first quotation, and the rest appears later in the same order. "wrote in an email interview" is supported. Supported.

11. D: "The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether its log could show the status of each repair."
    S: "It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available."
    Difference: "its" is neuter singular and refers to Svale's log, the same thing as "the log". The draft makes no claim of comparison with other suppliers. Supported.

### "The maintenance team designed its own categories"

12. D (heading): "The maintenance team designed its own categories"
    S: "The maintenance team designed its categories"; "The categories were ours".
    Supported.

13. D: "The team kept telephone reporting open for residents."
    S: "kept telephone reporting open for residents."
    Supported.

14. D: "“The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log,” Lind wrote."
    S: The second sentence of the first quotation, exact. The interview was by email.
    Supported.

15. D: "Svale also configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions."
    S: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions."
    Supported.

16. D: "Lind also offered advice about that work."
    S: "We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts."
    Difference: The draft calls the statement "advice". The source gives a first-person conditional about her own next building. **Finding 2.**

17. D: "“We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”"
    S: The same quotation, exact.
    Supported. It is attributed to Lind by the preceding sentence.

### "Median assignment time fell, but the note does not credit software"

18. D (heading): "Median assignment time fell, but the note does not credit software"
    S: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    Difference: "fell" describes the later period's lower median, which is a sequence and not a cause. The heading keeps the non-attribution. "does not credit" means the same as "does not attribute the difference to". It does not turn assignment time into completion time. The body carries the workload qualification. Not a finding.

19. D: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says 31 repair reports were entered."
    S: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered."
    Difference: "dated" is the natural reading of the appositive date. Supported.

20. D: "The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
    S: "It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
    Supported.

21. D: "The median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period."
    S: The same sentence, verbatim.
    Supported.

22. D: "The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    S: The same sentence, verbatim.
    Supported.

23. D: "There are no measurements of cost, resident satisfaction or completion time."
    S: "There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements."
    Supported.

### "Lind would repeat the trial, with an extra week to prepare"

24. D (heading): "Lind would repeat the trial, with an extra week to prepare"
    S: "I would choose to do the trial again. … but I would leave an extra week for preparation."
    Supported. The conditional and the reservation are kept.

25. D: "Lind's assessment is not an inference from the figures."
    S: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures."
    Supported.

26. D: "“I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”"
    S: The same quotation, exact.
    Supported.

27. D: "She did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
    S: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
    Pronoun: "She" is third person singular with feminine natural gender. The source refers to Lind as "Her final quotation is her actual … assessment", which supports it. Supported.

    Difference: "Elm Quay" stands for the team, a supported metonymy (see row 8). "will check" is presupposed by "will decide after checking". Supported.

    S: "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."

- Source: "Having one view of the reports helps us" (Lind's assessment). "It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial." "The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents."
- What differs:
  - The thing named: the source says "reports"; the title says "repairs", with no scope limit.
  - Whose assertion: the source's "one view" is Lind's; the title makes it the narrator's.
- Concrete case: during the trial, emergencies and repairs ordered before the trial are still handled outside the log. The material leaves this open; it says only that the note's count excludes them. In that case the reports entered in the log are in one view, so Lind's statement holds. But the trial did not put the two buildings' repairs in one view, so the title fails. No supplied statement excludes this case.

  - Line 19: "Lind also offered advice about that work."
- Source: "I would set that time aside before the next building starts." and "I would leave an extra week for preparation." Also "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
- What differs: The draft gives her statement the speech act of advising others. The source's wording is a first-person conditional, "I would …", tied to "the next building". Read that way, it is her own plan for Elm Quay.

The material supplies nothing that excludes this case. There, "offered advice" attributes a recommending stance she did not take. None. No quotation or passage is translated.

Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body, quotations and link text has been accounted for.

- Finding 1 (title scope: "repairs" versus "reports").
- Finding 2 ("advice" framing of Lind's conditional, lines 7 and 19).

arguments.content:
# Source comparison report: "Elm Quay's trial puts repairs in one view"

Draft: scratch/write-run.9ylQ/draft.md
Material: work/source.md
Draft language: en_US. Source language: English. No quotation is translated, so there are no translation findings. All findings below are source-support findings.

The byline "By Thomas Barregren" comes from the invocation, not from the material. It is excluded, as instructed.

## 1. Claim accounting

Each entry gives the draft passage (D), the source passage (S) in the source's own words, and the comparison.

### Title

1. D: "Elm Quay's trial puts repairs in one view"
   S: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately." / "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information." / Lind: "Having one view of the reports helps us"
   Comparison: "Repairs" is shorthand for the repair reports that the log collects, and the log shows "the status of each repair". The title makes no claim that every repair was included. Lind's present-tense "helps us" supports the present tense. Supported.

### Standfirst

2. D: "Elm Quay Housing's maintenance team spent eight weeks testing a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two buildings."
   S: "In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings." / "It chose Svale Systems" / "The trial lasted eight weeks."
   Comparison: Same subject, scope and duration. Supported.

3. D: "Its supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week of preparation."
   S: "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind" / "I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation."
   Comparison: The stance, the conditional "would" and the reservation all survive. The subject differs. "Its supervisor", with "its" referring to the maintenance team, presents Lind as the team's single supervisor. The source only says she is "maintenance supervisor", and nothing in the material makes her the only one. **Finding F1.**

4. D: "This case shows what the preparation took, what the trial figures show and what they leave open."
   Comparison: This is the author's framing of the article. It rests on the supported passages about categories, configuration, training, the trial note and the missing measurements. No finding.

### Opening paragraph

5. D: "In September 2025, the maintenance team at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats, decided to test a shared repair log in two of its buildings."
   S: "Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings."
   Comparison: "Two of its buildings" uses the possessive of association: buildings Elm Quay manages. That holds under any ownership arrangement the material allows. Dropping "own" makes the draft less specific without making it false. Supported.

6. D: "The trial that followed lasted eight weeks."
   S: "The trial lasted eight weeks."
   Comparison: The trial coming after the September decision is the natural chronology, and the dated note of 4 December 2025 is consistent with it. Supported.

7. D: "It left the team with a first set of figures, advice about preparation and a question to settle before it goes further."
   S: The trial note figures / Lind: "I would set that time aside before the next building starts." / "but I would leave an extra week for preparation." / "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
   Comparison: "First" means initial and does not promise further figures. "Advice" is a fair name for Lind's first-person "I would set that time aside" and "I would leave an extra week". The "question to settle" matches the pending check on larger repairs. Supported.

### Heading: "Elm Quay wanted its shifts to share one picture"

8. S: "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."
   Comparison: The wish belongs to the maintenance team, and the heading gives it to Elm Quay. The source calls the team Elm Quay's "own maintenance team", and the brief makes Elm Quay the acting party, so this metonymy is supported in the same way the source treats the team's decision as Elm Quay's. "Share one picture" says the same as "see the same information". Supported.

### Section: Elm Quay wanted its shifts to share one picture

9. D: "Before the trial, telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
   S: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
   Comparison: "Previously" and "before the trial" cover the same time. Both leave the scope unstated in the same way, and both imply the same change. Supported.

10. D: "'We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done,' maintenance supervisor Maya Lind wrote in an email interview."
    S: "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done." / "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind" / "All interviews occurred by email"
    Comparison: The quotation is verbatim, the title is exact, and "wrote in an email interview" is supported. Supported.

11. D: "The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether its log could show the status of each repair."
    S: "It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available."
    Comparison: "Its log" means Svale's log, which is the same thing as "the log". The draft makes no claim about comparing suppliers. Supported.

### Heading: "The maintenance team designed its own categories"

12. S: "The maintenance team designed its categories" / Lind: "The categories were ours"
    Comparison: "Own" is supported by "ours". Supported.

### Section: The maintenance team designed its own categories

13. D: "The team kept telephone reporting open for residents."
    S: "kept telephone reporting open for residents"
    Comparison: Identical. Supported.

14. D: "'The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log,' Lind wrote."
    S: "The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log."
    Comparison: This is the second sentence of the first quotation, verbatim. Splitting it from its first sentence welds nothing together and changes no meaning. Supported.

15. D: "Svale also configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions."
    S: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions."
    Comparison: The count and the actor are the same. "In" and "during" two sessions mean the same thing. Supported.

16. D: "Lind also offered advice about that work."
    S: "We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts."
    Comparison: The draft uses "that work" for the category and setup work, and the quotation that follows fixes the referent. Calling a first-person "I would set that time aside" advice is fair. Supported.

17. D: "'We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.'"
    S: Identical.
    Comparison: Verbatim. Supported.

### Heading: "The trial note does not credit software for quicker assignment"

18. S: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    Comparison: The non-attribution is correct, and the heading keeps assignment separate from completion. The heading does, however, presuppose "quicker assignment" in general, where the source measures only a change in the median. **Finding F2.**

### Section: The trial note does not credit software for quicker assignment

19. D: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says 31 repair reports were entered. The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
    S: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
    Comparison: The date format is en_US. "It" is resolved to the note, which is the grammatical antecedent in the source. Supported.

20. D: "The median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period."
    S: Identical in substance.
    Comparison: The measure is assignment, not completion. Supported.

21. D: "The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    S: Identical.
    Comparison: Supported.

22. D: "There are no measurements of cost, resident satisfaction or completion time."
    S: "There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements."
    Comparison: Supported.

### Heading: "Lind would repeat the trial, with an extra week to prepare"

23. S: "I would choose to do the trial again. ... but I would leave an extra week for preparation."
    Comparison: The conditional and the reservation are preserved. Supported.

### Section: Lind would repeat the trial, with an extra week to prepare

24. D: "Lind's assessment does not rest on the figures."
    S: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures."
    Comparison: "Rest on" is a claim about what Lind's own view is based on. The source sentence can be read two ways. It may say that her assessment was not derived from the figures, or it may say that the quotation is her real statement and not something inferred from the figures on her behalf. On the second reading, the source does not say what her assessment is based on. **Editorial question / Finding F3.**

25. D: "'I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.'"
    S: Identical.
    Comparison: Verbatim. The hedge, the "but" and the reservation survive. Supported.

26. D: "She did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
    S: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
    Comparison: Identical. The pronoun is covered in section 2. Supported.

### Heading: "Elm Quay will check larger repairs before deciding"

27. S: "the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
    Comparison: The thing checked has changed. The source checks how the categories work for larger repairs, while the heading says Elm Quay will check the larger repairs themselves. **Finding F4.**

### Section: Elm Quay will check larger repairs before deciding

28. D: "The trial has not yet been expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs."
    S: "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
    Comparison: "Its categories" means the team's, which is supported by "designed its categories". What will be decided is left unstated, as in the source. Supported.

29. D: "Operations managers considering a shared repair log of their own can read the [implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist)."
    S: "The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial."
    Comparison: The link text and the verb "read" describe the destination accurately, and the draft makes no booking or trial claim. Supported.

## 2. Pronoun accounting (person, number, natural gender)

- "Its supervisor" (standfirst): third person singular, non-personal, referring to the maintenance team. It carries no natural gender. The definiteness problem it creates is F1.
- "what they leave open" (standfirst): third person plural, referring to the trial figures. Supported.
- "which manages", "its buildings" (paragraph 1): third person singular, non-personal, referring to Elm Quay Housing. Supported.
- "It left the team" (paragraph 1): third person singular, referring to the trial. Supported.
- "before it goes further" (paragraph 1): third person singular, non-personal, referring to the team or the trial. Either reading matches "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide". Supported.
- "its shifts" (heading): third person singular, referring to Elm Quay. Supported (item 8).
- "its log" (section 1): third person singular, referring to Svale Systems. Supported.
- "its own categories", "its categories" (heading 2, final section): third person singular, referring to the team. Supported.
- "We", "ours", "us", "I" inside quotations: these are Lind's verbatim words and match the source exactly.
- "She" (final section of Lind's part): third person singular, referring to Maya Lind. It asserts female natural gender, which the source supports: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment." Supported.
- "their own" (final paragraph): third person plural, referring to operations managers. It carries no gender. Supported.

No pronoun asserts only grammatical gender. English has no grammatical gender on these referents.

## 3. Quotation check (quotations.md)

All four quoted passages are verbatim. Splitting the first interview quotation into its two sentences, placed in adjacent sections, keeps its meaning and joins no separate remarks together. No hedge, stance or reservation is removed or added. Lind's reservation ("but I would leave an extra week for preparation") survives. The quotations are in the source language, so no translation check applies.

## 4. Findings (source-support; no translation findings)

**F1: Standfirst: "Its supervisor" makes Lind the team's single supervisor.**
- Draft: "Its supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week of preparation."
- Source: "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind"
- What changed: "Its supervisor" is definite and identifies the supervisor of the maintenance team. The source gives only her job title.
- Case: The team has one supervisor per shift, say a morning and an evening supervisor, and Lind is one of them. The source statement holds and the draft fails. No supplied statement rules this out.
- Smallest repair: "Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind would run the trial again, with an extra week of preparation."

**F2: Heading drops "median" from the comparison of assignment times.**
- Draft heading: "The trial note does not credit software for quicker assignment"
- Source: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period."
- What changed: The heading presupposes that assignment was quicker in general. The source measures only the median of the note's counted reports, which exclude emergencies and work ordered before the trial. The base contract requires the qualification to be kept in headings.
- Case: The median fell from three to two working days, but a few long delays during the trial meant assignment was not quicker overall, for example on average. The source holds and the heading's unqualified "quicker assignment" fails.
- Smallest repair: "The trial note does not credit software for the shorter median assignment time"

**F3: Editorial question: "Lind's assessment does not rest on the figures."**
- Draft: "Lind's assessment does not rest on the figures."
- Source: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures."
- What differs: The draft makes a claim about what Lind's view is based on. The source sentence may only establish that the quotation is her real statement and not something inferred from the figures on her behalf.
- Case: Lind took the lower median into account when forming her view, while the quotation is still her actual words and not an inference drawn by the publisher. The source (on that reading) holds and the draft fails. The source's wording does not settle between the two readings, so this is reported as an editorial question rather than a clear defect.
- Smallest repair, keeping the source's own wording: "Lind's assessment is not an inference from the figures."

**F4: Heading changes what will be checked.**
- Draft heading: "Elm Quay will check larger repairs before deciding"
- Source: "the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
- What changed: The thing checked becomes the larger repairs themselves, rather than how the categories work for them.
- Case: The team reviews only whether its categories fit larger repairs and never inspects the repairs themselves. The source holds, while the heading, read as checking the repairs (for example their quality or progress), fails. The body sentence is correct.
- Smallest repair: "Elm Quay will test its categories on larger repairs before deciding"

## 5. Observation outside claim support (not a finding)

The brief says the publisher is the supplier and that the case "is not independent journalism". The draft does not claim independence, and supplier narration stays in the third person. Whether the page needs a supplier-published disclosure is an editorial and publishing question, not a question of source support, so it is not reported as a defect here.

## 6. Completion status

The comparison is complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body, quotations and link is accounted for, along with all pronouns. There are no translation findings.

Unresolved findings: F1 (standfirst "Its supervisor"), F2 (heading "quicker assignment" without "median"), F3 (editorial question on "does not rest on the figures") and F4 (heading "check larger repairs"). All four are open. Repairs are proposed, but none has been applied.
